_meta.directives: Fiche recentrée sur le nom (2026-10-03), passe de correction : chaque piste d'origine est attribuée à qui la porte et citée à la page dans les notes de sa source ; aucune n'est retenue comme la bonne. Ne pas étendre sans source dédiée.

oralTraditions.claim: The origin narrative of the Bambara dynasties tells of two brothers, Baramangolo and Niangolo, pursued by an enemy and without a canoe, who crossed the river thanks to an enormous catfish, the m'polio, which saved them just in time. Baramangolo then asks the Buare, Soninke of Ségou, for refuge, and they grant him a separate territory, while Niangolo builds a fortified town at Baïko.
oralTraditions.context: Historical synthesis published by UNESCO, French edition of 1999

oralTraditions.claim: The Coulibaly are said to come from Dyogo, a village near Ségou.
oralTraditions.carrier: Des griots que Molinie ne nomme pas
oralTraditions.collector: Molinie, officier de la marine française, en 1959
oralTraditions.context: Account taken from a dictionary written for Europeans posted in French West Africa, cited second-hand in a 2017 thesis that warns against its unfounded generalisations

oralTraditions.claim: The npolyo catfish, the fish of the river-crossing narrative, is among the Coulibaly taboos; the senior branch, that of Niangolo, also forbids itself the lion and the hippopotamus. A folk etymology of the name Kasanbara, borne by Dogon of Bandiagara and Bambara of Mopti and held to be equivalent to Coulibaly, derives it from kásaa ń bàra, "I smell of fish", and features a younger Coulibaly brother who ate a catfish. The same dictionary notes a common origin of the Coulibaly and the Keïta, and gives the motto "Masa Kuru ni Masa Donde!" as that of Biton Coulibaly.
oralTraditions.collector: V. Vydrine et A. Davydov, dont les matériaux sont publiés dans le dictionnaire des noms de clan et dans un mémoire de 2017
oralTraditions.context: Dictionary notes, with no indication of place or informant

oralTraditions.claim: Other narratives bring the Coulibaly from the south bank of the river, and even from Kong, and have them cross the river, for example on a catfish.
oralTraditions.collector: E. A. Bogacheva, qui les résume sans nommer de conteur
oralTraditions.context: Narratives summarised in Russian in a 2017 university thesis

linguisticReconstructions.claim: The dictionary of Mandinka clan names writes the name Kùlibàli, with the form Kùlubàli, and defines it only as a clan name, without giving it a meaning.

One explanation derives the name from the crossing of the river without a canoe: Koulibali would come from kulu, "canoe", and the privative bali. The source that gives it adds at once that there are others.

A 2017 study proposes reading the "without a canoe" explanation in the opposite sense: it could refer to ancestors who did not cross and remained on the north bank of the Niger, to which the study historically links the Coulibaly, with Koulikoro, Bamako and Kaarta. The study also places Ségou there, which the UNESCO synthesis nevertheless locates on the right bank, to the south.

Another reading starts from the forms Kudubali or Kurubali, which would contain kuluba, "the great hill", like the hill of Koulouba in Bamako. The 2017 study that proposes it considers this translation very plausible and ranks it among the probable learned etymologies, while noting that the name cannot be traced with certainty to any place name.

casteOrSocialFunction.value: The dictionary of jamuw gives the entry Kùlibàli the status hɔ́rɔn, then tontigi among the Bamana, Maninka and Minianka, then numu (blacksmith) in Wassoulou. The jamu thus carries both a free condition and, depending on the area, a hereditary artisanal function.

sources.title: EthniAfrica — fiche du peuple Bambara, organisation clanique
sources.notes: Taken from the "Clan organisation" chapter of the fiche of the Bambara people.

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Appendix of clan names of the Bamadaba, the electronic Bambara-French dictionary of the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA), pointed out by Vydrin in Mandenkan 63, 2020, pp. 89-110. Complete file consulted. The entry Kùlibàli gives the form Kùlubàli, the Bambara, Malinke, Minianka, Fulani, Kagoro and Soninke groups, the statuses hɔ́rɔn, then tontigi among the Bamana, Maninka and Minianka, and numu (blacksmith) in Wassoulou, the npolyo catfish among the taboos, the lion and the hippopotamus for the senior branch of Niangolo, and the motto of Biton Kulibali; it gives no meaning to the name. The joking pairs of this fiche are carried by the entries Kéyità and Fófana, which name Kulibali; the entry Kéyità also notes a common origin with Kulibali, and the entry Kásanbàra gives Kùlibàli as its equivalent. Joking ties are not always reciprocal from one entry to another: each pair is cited from the entry that carries it, which may be that of the other name.

sources.title: Pouvoir, places et filiation : les senankuya au Mali
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, Cahiers de praxématique, number 38, 2002, pp. 175-197. Field survey in Mali. It states what the pact requires: the relationship holds in perpetuity for all descendants of the two lineages, marriage between them is prohibited — unevenly applied today, it specifies — and mutual aid is owed without reserve. Cited for the obligation itself; it does not name the pair of this fiche, which the entries cited alongside it carry.

sources.title: Pactes, alliances et plaisanteries. Pratiques locales, discours global
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, and Smith, Étienne, Cahiers d'études africaines, number 184, 2006, pp. 687 ff. Cited for the caution it carries: the idea that joking kinship soothes conflicts is treated there as a hypothesis inherited from Radcliffe-Brown and taken up by conflict-resolution studies, hence as a discourse to be analysed and not as a measured effect. The first page is verified; the last page is not.

sources.title: Manden Charter, proclaimed in Kurukan Fuga, Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, UNESCO
sources.notes: Inscription of 2009. The entry describes a charter proclaimed at the beginning of the thirteenth century by the founder of the Mali empire and an assembly of sages, whose words are transmitted orally from father to son within Malinke clans. It does not mention sanankuya.

sources.title: Charte de Kurukan Fuga : mémoire et communauté, Amadou Saïbou Adamou, Magana, 2023
sources.notes: Cites article 7 of the charter: "Sanankunya (joking cousinage) and Tanamanyöya (a form of totemism) are instituted among the Mandenkas." Places the oral assembly around 1236 and specifies that the text was reconstituted by griots during a seminar at Kankan, in Guinea, in 1998, then translated into French and published in 2008.

sources.title: The World Won't Listen: The Mande Hunters' Oath and Human Rights in Translation, Gregory Mann, Humanity, 2022
sources.notes: Notes that the celebration of these charters has aroused scepticism among those who question their origin, and therefore their age, and refers to the work of Jan Jansen, who reads them as interventions in a disputed cultural politics.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, V : L'Afrique du XVIe au XVIIIe siècle — chapitre 12, Du Niger à la Volta
sources.notes: UNESCO, ed. B. A. Ogot, 1999; chapter by M. Izard and J. Ki-Zerbo. Printed pages: joking kinship between Koulibali (Kurubari) and Keita or Touré, given as an indication of very ancient relations between Bambara and Malinke, and the narrative of the two brothers Baramangolo and Niangolo crossing the river without a canoe thanks to an enormous catfish, then Baramangolo's refuge among the Buare of Ségou, on the right bank of the Niger (p. 372); the explanation of the name by kulu, "canoe", and bali, privative, with the mention that there are others (p. 372, note 7); Kaladian Koulibali and Mamari Koulibali (1712-1755), great-grandson of Baramangolo (p. 374); the origin of the nickname Biton (p. 375).

sources.title: Les noms de clan du Manden (jamu) dans les sources africaines, occidentales et arabes
sources.notes: Bogacheva, E. A., bachelor's thesis, Saint Petersburg State University, 2017, in Russian; supervised by A. Davydov, reviewed by V. Vydrin. Entry Kásanbàra: the folk etymology through kásaa ń bàra and the younger Coulibaly brother who ate a catfish, with no indication of provenance (p. 80). Entry Kùlibàli, pp. 94-96: the npolyo catfish among the clan's taboos (p. 95); the origin at Dyogo, near Ségou, after Molinie 1959, the narratives of a crossing from the south bank, the inverse reading of the "without a canoe" explanation and that through kuluba, "the great hill" (p. 96). The data without indication of provenance come there, according to the author, from materials gathered by V. Vydrin and A. Davydov, with no place or informant. Molinie, a naval officer, was writing a dictionary intended for Europeans posted in French West Africa and relied on griots whom he does not name; the thesis warns against his generalisations. A bachelor's thesis is not a peer-reviewed publication: it is cited for the testimonies it relays.

gaps.reason: Coulibaly transcribes the Mandinka Kulibali, which the dictionary of jamuw also writes Kùlubàli and which the Histoire générale de l'Afrique gives in the form Kurubari. None of these spellings corresponds to a distinct lineage of origin in the sources consulted.
